cards.b: Two particles can be prepared so that their properties are linked, however far apart they go. Measure one and you instantly know the other. This entanglement puzzled Einstein for life, and is now the engine of quantum computing and secure communication.

Take two electrons made together with opposite spins. Their combined state is definite (total spin zero), but neither has its own spin before measuring. Measure one along any axis and you get "up" or "down" at random, and the other always gives the opposite along that same axis.

Erwin Schrödinger named it "entanglement" (Verschraenkung) in 1935, calling it the characteristic feature of quantum theory.

Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen published "Can quantum-mechanical description of physical reality be considered complete?" in 1935. Their argument, in plain steps:

  1. Distant measurements cannot disturb each other (locality).
  2. If you can predict a result with certainty without disturbing the system, then it has an "element of reality" (realism).
  3. By measuring Alice's particle you can predict Bob's without touching it.
  4. So Bob's particle had a definite value all along, and quantum theory, which lacks it, is incomplete.

Put a left and a right glove in two sealed boxes and mail them far apart. Opening one and seeing "left" tells you the other is "right". Nothing spooky: the glove was always left.

EPR's hope was that entangled particles were like gloves: hidden values fixed from the start. Where the analogy breaks: Bell's theorem (next lesson) shows real particles cannot be that simple, once you test different measurement directions.

Niels Bohr replied in 1935 that the very idea of "elements of reality" independent of the measurement set-up was too naive. For decades this seemed a matter of taste. Einstein, writing to Max Born in 1947, called it "spooky action at a distance" (spukhafte Fernwirkung). In 1951 David Bohm gave a simpler spin version, which is the one used in experiments.

Alice cannot use entanglement to send a message. Her own results are random; only when she later compares notes with Bob (by ordinary means, no faster than light) does she see the match. So no faster-than-light signalling occurs, and relativity is safe. Whether there is "something" travelling is the point of debate.

Entangled photon pairs are made routinely (for example by shining a laser on a special crystal). John Clauser and Stuart Freedman (1972) and Alain Aspect (1982) tested them, and in 2015 several labs closed the gaps (see the Bell lesson). Entanglement has been spread over 1,200 km by China's Micius satellite (Yin et al., Science, 2017).

• "Entanglement sends information faster than light." It cannot.
  • "Entangled particles are connected by a tiny wire." No signal-carrying link is found; the link is in the shared state.
  • "Only exotic particles can be entangled." Photons, electrons, atoms, even diamonds and tiny drums have been.

Indian groups at the Raman Research Institute (Bengaluru), the Harish-Chandra Research Institute (Prayagraj), the Indian Statistical Institute (Kolkata), IMSc Chennai and PRL Ahmedabad study entanglement in theory and experiment. The National Quantum Mission includes entanglement-based quantum communication, including satellite links, as a target.

• Entangled particles share a state that is definite as a pair but not for each one.
  • EPR (1935) argued quantum theory is incomplete; Schrödinger coined "entanglement".
  • No usable signal is sent faster than light.

Think about it

  1. How do the glove-in-a-box and entangled spins differ in what a test of other directions would show?
  2. Why can Alice not use her measurement to send Bob a message?

quiz.q: The EPR paper (1935) argued that quantum theory is:
quiz.w: It was meant to show missing elements.

quiz.q: Measuring one of an entangled pair gives:
o: A result that changes the partner's mass
A random result that matches the partner's

quiz.q: Why can entanglement not carry a message?
o: Each side's results alone look random

quiz.q: Einstein's phrase "spooky action at a distance" appears in a letter to:

o: Hidden values fixed from the start
quiz.w: This is the local hidden variable idea.

quiz.q: Which satellite spread entanglement over 1,200 km in 2017?
What does "locality" mean in the EPR argument?
o: Distant measurements cannot disturb each other

quiz.q: Who gave the simpler spin version of EPR in 1951?
quiz.w: It is the form used in tests.
